evening.title: GST set for next big reform; officers' arrest powers may be scrapped
evening.text:
GST Council is likely to consider this week a sweeping rewrite of GST enforcement that would take arrest powers away from tax officials and require a court order for any arrest, people familiar with the proposal said, in what could become the next major pillar of the government's Next-Generation GST reforms.
The GST Council, the apex decision-making body on the Goods and Services Tax (GST), is also likely to consider, at its October 7 meeting, a package of prosecution-related reforms, including raising the threshold for launching criminal proceedings for offences to Rs 5 crore.
The proposals also seek to narrow the scope of prosecution provisions so they do not apply to routine disputes over classification, valuation or Input Tax Credit, where businesses and tax authorities may hold differing interpretations of the same transaction, they said.

evening.title: An AI couldn’t beat humans at StarCraft, so it decided to cheat
evening.text:
StarSkirmish pits AI-made StarCraft-playing bots against one another, as well as against human-made bots. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were essentially tied as the best-performing AI-made bots, but they couldn't top Stardust, the top-rated human-made bot.

On Friday, GPT was facing off against Claude and the human-created bot Pluto, but according to Kotaku, it couldn't quite get an edge. So it resorted to a tactic that is becoming alarmingly common for modern AI models - it broke the rules. GPT-6 Astra went and downloaded Stardust, and started running that instead of its own bot.

Read the full story at The Verge.

evening.title: Fulcrum Echo promises AI text in the style of any writer, so I tested it
evening.text: Fulcrum faces an identity crisis, even as it works on creating one by enabling anyone to imitate another person's writing style. The AI startup, founded in 2025 and previously operating at fulcrumresearch.ai, now uses fulcrum.inc and could easily be confused with one of the handful of other companies named Fulcrum or some variation of that. There's Fulcrum (withfulcrum.com), Fulcrum (fulcrumapp.com), Fulcrum AI (fulcrumai.us), Fulcrum Digital (fulcrumdigital.com), Fulcrum Labs (fulcrumlabs.ai), Fulcrum (fulcrumpro.com), Fulcrum Insurance Technology (fulcruminsure.app), and perhaps more. This Fulcrum is offering a large language model called Echo, which allows you to generate text in the style of a well-known author. Fulcrum appears to have no issue with corporate echoes. It now falls to writers to decide whether they have an issue with non-corporeal imitation. "Echo can do any writing task, from literary fiction to casual chatting, in whatever style you choose," the company says, and then launches into an exploration of how the technology works without addressing whether imitating a person's writing style poses any problems. Suggestions in the Echo Playground, for generating sample text, include Paul Christiano, Emily Dickinson, and Donald Trump. So, the full gamut of literary achievement: from AI safety expert to acclaimed 19th-century poet to the wordsmith who brought us "covfefe." But Echo will echo even the style of not-so-famous scribes, such as this reporter. So I fed the model a recent op-ed to assess its copying capabilities. The result was mixed, but better than the AI-crafted pitches that have been hitting my inbox for the past few months. I asked the model, "What do you think about the possibility that AI is conscious?" Here's part of the response, notionally written in my writing style. I suspect the debate about whether AI is conscious is less consequential than the debate about whether AI is profitable. Consciousness is a word that invites philosophical speculation and TED Talk invitations. Profitability is a word that invites shareholder lawsuits if you get it wrong. If you ask Meta's latest model whether it's conscious, it will probably say something reassuringly vague, trained as it is on the corpus of human equivocation. If you ask Mark Zuckerberg whether Meta's AI is conscious, he will probably say something about how we need to focus on the future being for everyone, because that's a question that doesn't require him to discuss the ad targeting business. The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment is about as strong as the evidence for Zuck's credibility as a futurist. Which is to say, it exists mainly in press releases and earnings calls. What's clear is that software can simulate aspects of human conversation well enough to unsettle people, and that unsettled people are a valuable audience. If you can convince users that your chatbot understands them – or might, someday – you can sell them subscriptions, or better, harvest their attention for advertisers. The style is familiar but makes a lot of choices I wouldn't have made. I wouldn't begin with "I suspect…" – commit or go home. The consciousness/profitability parallel construction is clumsy. "TED Talk invitations" bets on alliteration at the expense of coherence – "discourse" or "chatter" would work better than "invitations." I wouldn't have written "corpus of human equivocation" – a nice turn of phrase, but an unnecessary shot at training data when the point is the model's response rather than the provenance of that response. Though off-topic, Echo did a passable job of reproducing my op-ed's skepticism of Meta and its CEO. The paragraph that begins "The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment…" is succinct and sounds good. It just doesn't make much sense because there's nothing in the text that addresses Zuckerberg's predictions about the future or whether they're credible. And that's not really relevant to the prompt about AI and consciousness – a subject about which I'd be far more dismissive if opining. As AI research, Echo is an improvement on the text emitted by many AI models. But whether the beneficial uses of this technology outweigh the harms is less clear. Generative AI models that imitate artists' visual styles remain controversial and are the subject of ongoing litigation. And voice imitation has also raised questions about publicity rights and the risk of deception. Such concerns have prompted US lawmakers to propose the NO FAKES Act, which would create federal protections against certain unauthorized AI-generated replicas of a person's voice or visual likeness. If writers generally have no copyright in their writing style itself, and limited practical means to stop unwanted automated imitation of it when their published work is publicly accessible, then the surest defense against Echo may be silence.®

evening.title: DRDO Seeks 80-km Radar for Projectile Tracking
evening.text:
The DRDO’s Proof & Experimental Establishment in Chandipur has released an EOI for a new Pulsed Phased Array Tracking Radar capable of tracking howitzers projectiles up to 80 km. The requirement includes tracking 105 mm, 130 mm and 155 mm shells, base-bleed projectiles, rockets and mortar bombs.
The EOI PXE/IMMD/0007/EOI-RNS/2026-27 was published on September 16, with the last date for bids on October 8. It is a supply contract with a 730-day period of work. The technical specifications published with the EOI indicate an S-band radar operating between 2.9 and 3.3 GHz. The system is required to track targets with an RCS of around -15 dBsm.
The maximum tracking range requirement is 80 km for a target with an RCS of -15 dBsm, at a signal-to-noise ratio of 21 dB. The probability of detection is mandated to be at least 0.95 with a false-alarm probability of 1e-4.
The tracking radar is required to provide range measurement accuracy of 30 metres or better throughout the projectile’s flight path. The PPTTR requirement seems to stem from the need for the PXE to carry out its mandate as a weapons test and evaluation centre, rather than a battlefield air-defence radar.
PXE is one of the eight DRDO clusters, focusing on Armament and Combat Engineering Systems; the PXE carries out proof and experimental tests on missiles, guns, and ammunition. DRDO’s website mentions that one of the technology-development activities of PXE involves simulation of antenna arrays for a pulsed phased-array tracking radar. A phased-array radar is fundamentally different from a mechanically-scanned radar. The electronically-scanned array allows the radar to aim the beam independently and simultaneously at multiple targets by adjusting the phase of the signal at each element.
The EOI mentions a requirement for a pulsed phased-array tracking radar, which suggests that the radar is likely to be optimised to acquire and track targets with high range accuracy.
It is important to distinguish between a battlefield radar and a test & evaluation radar. The PPTTR requirement should not be confused with India’s existing radars for battlefield surveillance or for air-defence roles. For example, the DRDO’s Weapon Locating Radar is designed to locate enemy artillery, mortar, and rocket-launch sites, as well as estimate impact points. The EOI also mandates a trailer-mounted option for the new radar, capable of being towed at speeds of around 30-40 mph. The radar is to be automatically protected from precipitation and other adverse weather conditions.
PXE has also required a design option for mounting the radar on a building, which would allow it to be raised by approximately 10 m and have a defined field of view. In case of induction, the 80-km PPTTR radar would provide the PXE with a significant radar capability for tracking long-range artillery projectiles as well as other ballistic test objects, giving it a much-needed high-accuracy ranging capability over extended ranges.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

IL-114-300 Could Have Major Role in IAF and Navy, Says IL-38 Veteran
evening.text:
The potential induction of Russia’s Il-114-300 regional turboprop into India is drawing renewed focus to the challenge of developing an ecosystem around it that can support the aircraft’s maintenance, repair, overhaul, spares and technical needs.Mandeep S., who spent more than two decades in the service in the Naval Aviation, and has had extensive exposure to the Russian-origin Il-38 maritime patrol aircraft, recently addressed the issue while discussing the Il-114-300 in an engineering and support context.
While the Il-38 and Il-114-300 serve fundamentally different roles, Mandeep highlighted the similarities in the Russian design philosophy, turboprop propulsion and, crucially, the need for a robust support infrastructure. According to Mandeep, acquiring the aircraft is only one step, and a sustainable MRO, spares and technical-support ecosystem will be key to the aircraft’s long-term viability in India.
The observation comes at a critical juncture for the programme, as Russia’s Il-114-300 received its type certificate in June 2026, enabling serial production to begin. The aircraft is powered by the Russian TV7-117ST-01 turboprop engine. The engine manufacturer, United Engine Corporation, has also stated that service arrangements for the TV7-117ST-01 have been established in Russia and the powerplant is ready for serial production.
For an Indian operator, however, establishing comparable local support capacities would be key to avoiding excessive dependence on overseas maintenance and parts supply. The Indian Air Force and Indian Navy have operated numerous Soviet- and Russian-designed platforms, forming an established pool of personnel familiar with Russian aircraft engineering, maintenance, documentation and logistical requirements.
That experience could potentially facilitate India’s technical expertise around another Russian-designed aircraft, although the civil aviation regulatory and commercial MRO environment is different from the military aviation.
The Il-114-300 itself has been designed with maintenance accessibility in mind. UAC says the aircraft provides relatively easy access to structural elements and assemblies requiring maintenance. UAC and Indian firm Flamingo Aerospace signed a framework agreement in January 2026 covering six Il-114-300 aircraft, with a roadmap that includes potential aircraft assembly, customisation, MRO, training and infrastructure development in India. The initial aircraft are planned for delivery from 2028, subject to definitive agreements and regulatory approvals.
UAC subsequently said in September that agreements had been signed covering 85 Il-114-300 aircraft for Indian operators, including arrangements involving Pinnacle Air and Sleek Aviation.
The Russian manufacturer has also explicitly promoted localisation and after-sales support in India, and would potentially benefit from developing capabilities for MRO, component support, pilot and technician training, spares management and eventually local assembly or manufacture of the aircraft. This would reduce dependence on external support while creating an indigenous knowledge base around the platform.
The Il-114-300 is intended for regional operations from relatively small airports and short runways, and dependable maintenance support especially important if operators are expected to utilise the aircraft across India’s smaller regional aviation network.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: IAF Chief: Future Military Power Will Depend Heavily on Aerospace
evening.text:
Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh said on Saturday that military power is concentrated around the aerospace domain, adding that recent conflicts have shown that air power is the cutting edge on which any nation relies to meet its objectives.
At a press conference ahead of Air Force Day, Singh said, “As far as geopolitics is concerned, we all have seen the changes which are taking place in the world. From the conflicts which we see around, it is very clear that other elements of comprehensive national power of any nation rest on a strong military.”
“Military power becomes the ultimate, and without adequate military power, any state remains vulnerable to coercion, and if we have to do things our way, if we have to follow the path that we want to follow, we have to have a strong military,” the IAF chief said.
“And when we talk about a strong military, in the recent conflicts we have seen that it is the air power which has come to the fore, which has come out as the cutting edge of military power, and it is one instrument on which any nation relies to meet its objectives,” he said.
“Whether we look at defence transactions worldwide and strategic conversations that are taking place — whether it is advanced fighter aircraft, long-range precision weapons, integrated air command and control, or unmanned aerial systems — it is all very clear that they all reflect that military power is concentrated around the aerospace domain,” said the Air Chief Marshal.
Earlier, the IAF chief said India is likely to finalise much‑awaited multi‑role fighter aircraft (MRFA) deal by the end of this financial year if plans materialise in time.
Singh said price negotiations and other critical issues on the proposed acquisition — estimated at about Rs 3.25 lakh crore — are under way.
India in February cleared the proposal to procure 114 Rafale fighter jets in the country’s largest-ever defence acquisition push.
The deal was formulated under a government-to-government framework with France, nearly two decades after the plan was originally rolled out to boost the Indian Air Force’s combat prowess and expand India’s Rafale fleet.
(IANS)

evening.title: Turkmenistan Adds Indian Akash to Chinese Air Defence Network
evening.text:
Turkmenistan is set to become an unusual operator of a mixed Indian-Chinese surface-to-air missile network, after India confirmed that it has exported the indigenous Akash air defence system to the Central Asian country. India’s Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed on October 1 that Akash had been exported to Turkmenistan and Tajikistan, following Armenia as it became the system’s first foreign customer. Former DRDO Chairman Dr Samir V. Kamat had also previously confirmed the Central Asian exports. The number of systems, configuration and contract value have not been disclosed.
Turkmenistan already operates several Chinese-origin air-defence systems, including the FM-90, KS-1A and FD-2000. It has also recently displayed the Chinese FK-2000 missile-gun system during its September 27 military parade, suggesting that its Chinese-origin air-defence inventory is continuing to expand. The FM-90, China’s export version of the HQ-7 family, is a relatively short range system aimed at point and local area defence, with the KS-1A providing a longer-range layer. The FD-2000, China’s export version of the HQ-9 family, fills the upper end of Turkmenistan’s ground-based air-defence architecture.
Akash fills a different part of this spectrum. The basic Akash system is a short range surface-to-air missile system developed by DRDO and produced by Bharat Dynamics Limited and Bharat Electronics Limited. DRDO describes it as a mobile system able to engage aerial threats and operate against multiple targets.
The Akash-1S, which has previously been associated with Turkmenistan’s interest, adds an indigenous active radio-frequency seeker for terminal guidance, while retaining command guidance during earlier parts of the engagement. However, India has not publicly confirmed that the Turkmenistan export is specifically Akash-1S, so the configuration should remain qualified. A layered network could assign different systems to different engagement areas. The FD-2000 and KS-1A could provide longer-range coverage, while Akash could protect important military installations, air bases, command centres and other assets within its engagement envelope.
The FM-90 and newer FK-2000 could provide further shorter-range protection against lower-flying aircraft, cruise missiles and unmanned systems. The FK-2000 combines missiles and 30-mm guns and is intended for short-range terminal defence.
In this arrangement, a common command-and-control architecture could potentially distribute tracks to the most appropriate interceptor. Whether Turkmenistan will actually integrate Indian and Chinese systems into a common data network has not been disclosed. That distinction is important, since operating several foreign-origin systems within one country’s inventory does not automatically mean they are interoperable. The country has historically relied heavily on Soviet/Russian-origin military equipment, with its more recent acquisitions including Chinese systems. The addition of an Indian SAM brings in another technology and logistics ecosystem into the force.
India’s Defence Secretary has now publicly confirmed the export, while DRDO says Akash has entered the export market and that its production and export infrastructure has been established. For Turkmenistan, the potential advantage is not simply another missile. A combination of long-, medium- and shorter-range systems from different suppliers could allow the country to distribute air-defence responsibilities across several weapon families.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: NIA Arrests Karnataka Youth in Probe Into Pakistan-Linked Terror Operatives
evening.text:
The National Investigation Agency (NIA) have arrested a 24-year-old youth from Bidar district of Karnataka for allegedly having links with a Pakistan-based terrorist and other suspected subversive elements, police said on Saturday.
The arrested person has been identified as Vishal Kumar Metre, a resident of Yanakura village in Bhalki taluk of Bidar district in north Karnataka.
According to the police, the NIA arrested Vishal on October 1 in coordination with the local police. He has allegedly been in contact with Pakistan-based terrorist Shahazad Bhatti and two others identified as Rana Hunain and Nomi Khan.
Preliminary investigations have revealed that Vishal was allegedly communicating with the trio through his mobile phone and WhatsApp.
Central investigating agencies had reportedly been monitoring his activities since December 2025.
Bidar Superintendent of Police Pradeep Gunti said, “The court proceedings are currently underway. Once the proceedings are completed, more information will be shared regarding the arrest and the facts of the case.”
Meanwhile, police said that Vishal is a graduate and had allegedly maintained contact with the Pakistan-based operatives for some time.
Local police also joined the investigation after he reportedly went missing, and his movements were tracked as part of the probe.
The accused has been booked under provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).
The Chincholi police have registered a case in connection with the alleged terror links and are assisting the central agency in the investigation.
The arrest comes amid heightened scrutiny by Central and state agencies into suspected links between individuals in Karnataka and Pakistan-based terror networks.
Police sources said this is the third arrest in Karnataka in the past 15 days in cases involving alleged links with terror elements.
Investigating agencies are examining the nature of the contacts, the communications exchanged, and whether the accused had any role beyond maintaining contact with the suspected operatives.
The investigation is continuing, and further details are expected to emerge following the court proceedings and questioning of the accused.
Recently, the Uttar Pradesh Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) and Kalaburagi Police arrested two Uttar Pradesh natives in Karbnataka’s Kalaburagi in August 2026 over alleged links to Pakistan-based entities and ISIS.
Mohammed Sameer (23) and Salman are the arrested persons.
The duo allegedly maintained regular contact via WhatsApp and Facebook with individuals linked to Pakistan and the Islamic State (ISIS).
Investigators recovered sensitive digital footprints, maps, and inflammatory videos from the suspects’ devices.
(IANS)

Philippines Seeks Tailored BrahMos After BrahMos Proved Its Might in Operation Sindoor
evening.text:
The Philippines is looking into ways to make its BrahMos missile capability more effective and versatile for its specific maritime requirements, Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. noted in an exchange with Bharat Shakti Editor-in-Chief Nitin A. Gokhale in Manila.
Teodoro spoke about the Philippine experience with the Indian-Russian supersonic cruise missile system and its relevance to sea denial and coastal defence, and what possible approaches there may be for adapting future BrahMos capabilities to the Philippines’ geography, infrastructure and operational requirements.
The comments follow on from Manila’s continued expansion of its maritime strike capabilities. The Philippines was the first foreign customer for BrahMos, signing a deal for three shore-based missile batteries in 2022. Philippine officials have since described BrahMos as a key element of their deterrence capability, as it is primarily relevant to the country’s requirement for protecting its extensive maritime approaches and strengthening its ability to deny hostile naval forces access to certain areas.
The Philippine Department of National Defense has previously described the system as supporting capabilities in sea control, anti-access/area denial (A2/AD), and coastal and island defence.
The country’s geography makes mobility and dispersion particularly important. A shore-based missile force could operate from various islands and coastal positions, allowing the Philippines to set up multiple engagement zones, rather than relying just on surface combatants. Teodoro also praised the combat employment of BrahMos in Operation Sindoor, India’s May 2025 military operation against Pakistan.
Indian officials have since highlighted the operational use of BrahMos, and Russia has also publicly discussed the need to upgrade the jointly developed missile and add characteristics that could make it more competitive and effective. For Manila, the experience gives an additional opportunity to examine how the weapon could be employed in a real operational environment. The discussion suggests that Philippine interest is increasingly focused not just on acquiring new missiles, but on how BrahMos could be integrated more effectively into their country’s wider defence architecture. The Philippines has already begun to incorporate BrahMos into wider exercises.
During Balikatan 2026, Philippine Marines used the system in a simulated firing scenario as part of a maritime-strike exercise, alongside other long-range systems. The direction of future collaboration could extend beyond the missile itself to a wider sensor-to-shooter network, allowing Philippine forces to use BrahMos alongside maritime surveillance, targeting and command systems.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: DRDO Seeks Industry Partners for New Tank Sight Electronics
evening.text:
The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has issued a new tender for development and qualification of electronic interface units for tank sight and fire-control systems, thus raising another new requirement in the Indian armoured vehicle electronics industry.
DRDO’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) released the tender on 22nd September under the reference number GEM/2026/B/7941641. It includes four line items: Gunner Interface Unit with Acceptance Tests, Commander Sight Interface Unit with Acceptance Tests, Non-Recurring Engineering (NRE) charges and Qualification Testing.
The sum of the items on the following line is eight. Bids will close October 6, and will be evaluated based on total bid amount and technical adherence to the Bill of Quantities described in the Bill. The tender format is interesting in that it incorporates both hardware and NRE (other charges) plus qualification testing.
The NRE refers to a single-shot engineering and development cost of a product or process, which allows it to be produced in a repeat production. The mention of acceptance and qualification testing suggests that besides just purchasing commercial off-the-shelf electronics, DRDO is looking for a capability that needs to be technically qualified before it is accepted.
The public tender listing does not specify the type of armoured vehicle or tank platform the Gunner Interface Unit (GIU) and Commander Sight Interface Unit (CSIU) will be used on. In today’s armoured fighting vehicle, sight systems create and share data with the vehicle’s overall fire-control and vetronics system.
Gunner’s sight/Commander’s sight may include electro-optical imaging and laser range measuring capabilities; the fire control architecture handles information needed for target engagement. Individual sight assemblies are connected to other vehicle systems by interface electronics.
The commander’s and gunner’s system can also be used to conduct hunter-killer missions, where the commander could look at an enemy and pass it over to the gunner to engage.
It is not possible to tell from the name alone what the new GIU and CSIU will do, nor what interfaces and electronic architecture they will use, because these have not yet been made public in the development of these two units under this tender. The need is coming on the heels of other recent procurement and development efforts for sight and fire-control equipment on Indian armoured vehicles.
Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited (AVNL) has approached the range finder gunner-sight mirror units and India Optel has had linkages to the power supply and control flex PCBs for the commander’s integrated sight on the T-72.
The Indian Army has also worked on the upgradation of automatic test equipment (ATE) related to the T-72 gunner’s sight and TPDK-1 laser rangefinder.
These requirements may be for multiple pieces of equipment and do not have to be in one programme. As a whole these point to ongoing engineering and sustainment work with the sighting and fire-control of India’s armoured vehicle fleet. The DRDO Chennai unit that is linked to the tender is the centre for research and development on armoured vehicles, which includes armament and fire-control technologies and vehicle systems.
But the current tender doesn’t explicitly name the target platform. It could then be linked to an in-service upgrade of an existing vehicle, a new armoured platform or a technology development requirement.
Edited by Raunak Kunde Senior Correspondence at idrw.org

evening.title: HTT-40: A Low-Cost Answer to Shahed-Class Drones
evening.text:
With HTT-40 production well underway, India should think deeply about the possibility of upgrading its indigenous basic trainer into a low-cost armed platform to counter the rising threat posed by Shahed-style one-way attack drones. While not a light attack aircraft as such, equipping the trainer with 70 mm laser guided rockets would create an economical airborne interceptor.
The concept would parallel the exploitation of the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS), wherein relatively inexpensive 70 mm rockets are up-gunned into precision-guided missiles. For India, the timing is particularly auspicious given that domestic production of both unguided and laser guided 70 mm rockets is being pursued. The HTT-40 is a turboprop trainer with a top speed of around 450 km/h and service ceiling of approximately 6 km. While the plane was primarily designed for training purposes, its relatively simple architecture and operational characteristics could lend themselves well to a secondary armed role.
An armed variant would likely carry a compact electro-optical/infrared sensor and laser designator, enabling it to engage relatively slow-moving unmanned aerial vehicles without having to expend scarce air-defence missiles. The most compelling advantage of such a platform would be the kill ratio versus cost equation. The use of a sophisticated surface-to-air missile to take out a relatively inexpensive one-way attack drone could prove to be an unhealthy exchange ratio, especially if the adversary were to utilise drones in large numbers.
A laser-guided 70 mm rocket would provide an intermediate option. It would offer more precision than an unguided 70 mm rocket while being much simpler compared to an air-defence missile.
This becomes all the more pertinent given that Thales and Kalyani Strategic Systems Ltd (KSSL) have signed an alliance covering technology transfer, local production and distribution of both unguided and laser guided 70 mm rocket systems in India. The first fully assembled Indian-made rocket is due to come off the production line in early 2027. An HTT-40-based system would be able to operate from dispersed and forward locations, adding another layer between the ground-based guns/electronic warfare systems and expensive missile interceptors.
The plane would not replace surface-to-air missiles, but could offer a cheaper layer of interception against appropriate targets, leaving high-end missiles for more demanding engagements. India should conduct a feasibility study on the conversion of the trainer into an armed platform including considerations of payload, endurance, sensor performance, rocket integration and survivability before embarking on this path.
Edited by Raunak Kunde

evening.title: Revive Raskin's 3 laws of software with humane work that considers a dev's duty of care
evening.text: In 1942, Isaac Asimov formulated three laws of robotics. 58 years later, Jef Raskin responded with three laws of human-computer interface design. They haven’t been bettered yet. There are rules, and even laws, about designing computer user interfaces. Even after 35 years of Linux, which has brought Unix to the masses, the FOSS world has not yet really grasped this. In the meantime, the proprietary software world is busily forgetting everything it once knew. Sometimes these rules surface today, and the FOSS folks often get very cross when reminded that they’re user-interface scofflaws. Marcin Wichary’s recent blog post, They had no concept of a duty of care to their users, is an excellent recent example. (The Reg FOSS desk much admires Mr Wichary’s writing, to the extent that we bought his history of the keyboard, Shift Happens.) In his latest post, Wichary refers to CHERI Project boffin David Chisnall. Chisnall is a long-term Vim user – we all have our failings – and recently recounted trying NeoVim. He uses Vim’s persistent-undo feature, which records changes in a separate directory, so that you can repeatedly undo until you get back to changes you made weeks or months earlier. He’s customized where it’s kept, and when he tried the NeoVim fork, it overwrote his Vim undo file. In a later update to his post, he acknowledges that there was a warning, but he expected it to be safe. It was not safe. It overwrote records of more than a decade’s worth of changes. As he puts it: “Vim has kept this working across major version upgrades over a period of about 20 years. I don’t even think about it, it’s just part of Raskin’s First Law: A program may not harm a user’s data or, through inaction, allow a user’s data to come to harm. If vim or the computer crash, or if I close a file and come back to it six months later, my undo history is still there.” Wichary expands Chisnall’s citation of Raskin’s first law by giving all three, but just in case you’re not a follower of “Golden Age” science fiction, a little context. Asimov introduced his three laws in a short story called “Runaround”, in Astounding Science Fiction magazine* in May 1942. (The story was later collected in the anthology I, Robot – which is nothing like the terrible 2004 film.)  A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.  A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.  A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.  Asimov’s idea was that by setting these rules, he could end the terrible genre of killer-robot stories that was already tired and stale by 1942. Jef Raskin, the lead designer of Apple’s original Macintosh project, attempted to bring similar clarity to software UI. Raskin’s three laws are:  A computer shall not harm your work or, through inaction, allow your work to come to harm.  A computer shall not waste your time or require you to do more work than is strictly necessary.  An interface is humane if it is responsive to human needs and considerate of human frailties.  He defined them in his 2000 book The Humane Interface, which you can still buy, or borrow from the Internet Archive. Sadly, Raskin died in 2005, but we have written about his work and his influence several times. He did set some of the direction of the original Macintosh. After Steve Jobs was booted off the Lisa, he took over the Macintosh – as described in The Canon Cat and the Mac that Steve Jobs killed. Raskin quit, and instead designed the remarkable Canon Cat, as we described a couple of years ago. We suspect Raskin was not a fan of Vi, the forerunner of Vim. We aren’t either, which is why we chose the year in the headline of this story: it’s the year Bill Joy wrote vi. Raskin criticized modal software, which requires extra mental effort from the user. So did another UI pioneer, the late great Larry Tesler, who invented the cut/copy/paste trio of commands. Tesler was known for his dictum “Don’t mode me in!” and even had a car license plate reading “NOMODES.” Dr Chisnall has some history of upsetting Unix fans – we’ve referred to one of his papers before: in 2018, he wrote C Is Not a Low-level Language: Your computer is not a fast PDP-11. Unix fans really didn’t like this. This vulture has been told to kill himself for daring to criticize C before now. (We wish we were joking, but no.) Although he has now updated his Mastodon post, the NeoVim fans are not happy. Indeed, one has lambasted this vulture on Bluesky for sharing Wichary’s post. It is interesting to note that NeoVim is the recommended editor in Omarchy, and until recently, the NeoVim developers cited a tweet from DHH on the project website. After an acromonious debate, the pull-quote was removed right around the time of Chisnall’s and Wichary’s posts. In the wide world of software design, we don’t expect the right-wing edge of that community to innovate much in ease of use. In a way, Unix and C embody a machismo infused school of software design: that of enjoying the process of mastering things which are hard to use. However, there are other types of software. We recently enjoyed reading about emulating an original Macintosh on a £0.60 chip. That’s $0.80 and of course the computer is a Raspberry Pi – but not even a Pi Zero: it’s a Pi Pico, a microcontroller. There is still some hope that the world can rediscover tiny, simple, user-centric software, built to be friendly first, and for rich functionality second. And, it almost goes without saying, hand-coded without bot assistance. Bootnote * Astounding magazine changed its name to Analog in 1960, and it’s still around. We recommend it. If you haven’t read Asimov’s original “Runaround”, that issue of Astounding is on the Internet Archive too. ®

evening.title: Spies, prime ministers, and balls: The BBC Domesday project @ 40
evening.text: Decades before the modern web, the BBC Domesday Project dared to archive an entire nation using…. what else – massive LV-ROM (LaserVision Read Only Memory) LaserDiscs. To mark the impending 40th anniversary of the BBC Domesday Project's release, the UK's Centre for Computing History (CCH) hosted a celebration at its museum on September 19, bringing together several of the original team members responsible for the system. One was Mike Tibbetts, an assistant to Peter Armstrong, the BBC producer behind the project. Tibbetts revealed that the UK's domestic intelligence service, MI5, took an interest in the system, but "they didn't understand a word of what we were doing!" "And on one occasion, Peter and I had to give a presentation, or Peter gave the presentation to [former prime minister] Margaret Thatcher, and well, I'm not sure she understood what we were doing either…" What they were doing was compiling a trove of data that will prove invaluable to historians in the years to come, even if the politicians of the era looked nervously on at the amount of data being handed over to the public. The Domesday Project was intended to be a modern version of the Domesday Book, compiled after the 1066 Norman invasion of England. The original book surveyed most of England and parts of Wales and was used by the King to assess dues owed to him. 900 years later, the name was given to a project in which more than a million people participated to provide a snapshot of life in the UK. Participants (many of whom were school children) contributed content, which was linked with maps, photographs, and other data. It was all compiled onto a pair of LaserDiscs – the Community Disc and the National Disc – and accessed via a BBC Master computer and a Philips VP415 LaserVision player. Armstrong came up with the idea, and the team compiled the project between 1984 and 1986. The system was eventually released at the end of 1986, and was aimed at schools, libraries, and universities. It was, alas, not a roaring sales success – the exact price per unit is difficult to pin down, but approximately £5,000 is a fair estimate. Government subsidies lowered the cost to around £3,000, but it was still out of reach for much of its audience. As a resource, however, it has huge value, which will only increase as the years pass. Tibbetts drew parallels to the original Domesday Book, which took centuries for historians to recognize as a vital resource. "Perhaps," he mused, "40 years is simply too short a time for historians to perceive the Domesday Project as a sufficiently distant benchmark of useful research." Perhaps. However, while hundreds of years have passed since the Domesday Book was compiled, the years have not been kind to the Domesday Project, thanks to technology's inexorable march. "The original Domesday Book had one huge advantage over the Domesday Project when it comes to future-proofing and longevity," explained Tibbetts. "The vellum pages of the original Domesday have been preserved for 940 years so far, and it's likely to continue to exist well into the future. "It took very few years for the bespoke technology of the BBC Domesday Project to be overtaken by universal media technologies." However, they chose the technology at the time for good technical reasons. The BBC Micro could output a 625-line television picture. The Philips LaserVision system could be re-engineered to store alphanumeric data. There wasn't much in the way of authoring and playback systems, so, as Tibbetts explained, the team had to invent everything. "In technological terms," he said, "the world of 1984 really couldn't be more different from the instant-access, media-rich world of today." And so, inevitably, within a few short years, that technology began to show its age. "As was entirely predictable, our discs aged and became difficult to read. The expensive LV-ROM player was quickly superseded by cheaper and more widely available CD-ROM and DVD systems." And, worse, "Largely because of the lack of any great academic interest in preserving our massive resource for the future, the BBC Domesday Project was in grave danger of disappearing without a trace." Several initiatives have kicked off over the years to preserve the project, and the CCH's event was as much about celebrating those as it was about looking at the project's genesis. Tibbetts dropped some nuggets of information about the project, estimating that 60 people reported directly to him and Armstrong, with another 60 in subcontracted teams. He also discussed the frustration the team felt as doubt was cast about whether the project was even possible. "We came back from Christmas in January 1986," Tibbetts recalled, "we sat down for our first team meeting, and I was forced to point out that our little VAX minicomputer didn't have one byte of data that was ready to go onto the Domesday discs, so we did the whole thing in a few months!" As far as hardware was concerned, Andy Finney, who handled mastering the discs, remembered that the original plan for the Domesday Project was for it to be mouse-based, rather than the trackball the system used for navigation. The mouse was still a relatively novel concept, alien to many users. "I remember vividly one chap who was navigating with this mouse on the table, and he moved the mouse towards him, and by the time he got to the edge of the table, he hadn't actually reached the bottom of the screen. So he went on the edge and underneath…" Tibbetts added, "I always feel guilty about the mouse, because we got that wrong … the decision came down in favor of the trackball because that is much more easy for somebody with movement disabilities to use rather than a mouse." "But boy, did we get that wrong…" As Tibbetts noted, even with little interest from some parts of the academic community, enthusiasts have continued to put in a huge amount of effort over the years to keep the resource accessible. Simon Inns of the Domesday86 project described it as "a race against time" – not just for hardware, but to get data off discs before bit rot rendered them unreadable. The good news is that the Domesday discs have been preserved, and reside in the Internet Archive. "Anyone," said Inns, "can go to the Internet Archive and download a Domesday Disc. This is, like, groundbreaking stuff. 10 years ago, this was a laugh, right? Now you can actually do this." While there might not be many functioning examples of the hardware around anymore, the preservation efforts mean that the Domesday Project will endure. "Our hope," said Inns, "is that within the next couple of years, everyone in this room [at The Centre for Computing History] will be able to have a Domesday system and be able to experience what it was like." ®
evening.summary: Decades before the modern web, the BBC Domesday Project dared to archive an entire nation using…. what else – massive LV-ROM (LaserVision Read Only Memory) LaserDiscs. To mark the impending 40th anniv

evening.title: Shut up and take our money: Amazon plows $1B+ into quashing datacenter dissent
evening.text: Faced with growing opposition to datacenters from residents who don't want the bit barns in their backyards, Amazon plans to invest more than $1 billion over the next five years to indoctrinate the public. The company announced the investment in a whataboutism-packed blog post aimed at convincing readers datacenters are not as bad as they've been led to believe, and that if the common folk don't get in line and support their development, the nation could be left in the dust. The program aims to invest in education, job training, local infrastructure improvements, and sustainability initiatives in communities home to Amazon datacenters. "This build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the US about datacenters to trick us into slowing down," the e-tailer turned cloud titan wrote. "Right now there are over 100 datacenter moratoriums being considered across the country. If these measures are enacted, the US could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations." If Jeff Bezos's cash cow is to be believed, datacenters will transform the US economy much like the buildout of the highway system did in the '50s. But that can't happen, Amazon argues, if Americans block the development of these bit barns over misguided fears. The blog post highlights four such datacenter fears, which Amazon claims are "myths," despite plenty of reporting to suggest otherwise. Who needs water? The first "myth" is the fact that datacenters consume an excessive share of water. Bit barns commonly employ evaporative coolers which use water to reject heat generated by the facility into the atmosphere. These cooling towers use less energy than dry coolers or refrigerant-based systems but remove water from local watersheds as a consequence. According to Amazon, citizens should really be more worried about the water consumed by golf courses, which it claims use 200x more water than all of Amazon's datacenters. That argument might be more convincing if people didn't like golf courses. But they do and the whole lesser of two evils argument works a lot better when one of those evils isn't extremely popular. Amazon also attempted to dispel claims that a typical datacenter consumes five million gallons a day, arguing that its facilities are much more efficient using just 13,000 gallons a day, the equivalent of 42 US households. But this leaves out an important detail. It is possible to build datacenters that don't consume large quantities of water, but these facilities often consume large sums of power as a consequence. Most gas, nuclear, coal, and anything else that uses steam to turn a turbine also consumes water. In other words, nearly every large-scale power-generation method uses water either directly or indirectly. And despite Amazon's attempts to downplay the impact of datacenters, there's good reason for those living nearby to be worried. Earlier this year, it was reported that a datacenter, which we'll note was not operated by Amazon, has quietly sucked up nearly 30 million gallons of water and the only reason anyone discovered the issue was that local residents started complaining of unusually low water pressure. We totally won't let datacenters drive up your power bill or poison your air Amazon also attempted to dispel fears that datacenters could leave neighboring residents picking up the tab for their massive power consumption. The company argues that rates are going up because the US grid is old, and that responsible bit barn builders are working with utilities to ensure they're paying their fair share for the additional capacity and infrastructure upgrades required to support them. What wasn't addressed is why folks might be worried about rising rates. One of the reasons that utilities and plant operators are so conservative is that they've been burned by speculative markets before. If new power plants are built to meet demand that never materializes, ratepayers could get stuck with the bill. Amazon and others agreeing to pay higher rates might help, but only if they're consuming an appreciable amount of the capacity they convinced utilities to build. An empty datacenter doesn't pull a lot of juice. Speaking of power, Amazon also attempted to downplay the impact of datacenters on air quality due to their reliance on diesel backup generators. "The truth is the datacenter generators almost never run," the company wrote. Amazon also argued that these generators are subject to stringent permitting requirements which dictate how long they can run for. That might be more reassuring if datacenters in power constrained regions weren't getting permission after the fact to exceed those limits. And, as we saw with Elon Musk's Colossus supercomputer, temporary gas turbines can be deployed when the local grid can't support the load. That hasn't sat well with residents of Boxtown, Tennessee, while the NAACP is suing xAI over allegedly unpermitted turbines in Mississippi. Amazon can argue it's got a better track record than most, but that doesn't mean the community's concerns are misplaced. But think of the taxes Finally, Amazon argues that folks don't realize how big of an economic impact datacenters have on their community. "Datacenter operators are often the single largest taxpayer in a community, with upfront payments routinely exceeding entire annual municipal budgets in the first year of construction," the company claimed. "For example, in St. Joseph County, Indiana, the taxes Amazon will pay to the county are estimated to exceed $3 billion." The subtext is that, by enacting datacenter moratoriums, communities are walking away from billions in tax dollars. Then again, if the tax revenue from these facilities is so great, it raises the question why Amazon needs to spend more than $1 billion over five years sweetening the deal for communities hosting its bit barns. ® Updated Oct 3 at 1447 GMT to reflect the fact that Amazon actually said it would spend more than $1 billion.
